title: Seeking feedback on my loyalty points app
body:
O.P.
Solo dev from Melbourne seeking feedback on my app, posting under the rules exception for apps built by users. Mods, if I've read that wrong feel free to bin this.
"What are my points worth", "Are rewards credit cards worth it" and "What's the best use of my points" comes up here and in other forums all the time. I used to track this stuff in a spreadsheet for my own use, but over the past few months have built it into an app called PointMate.
The key questions/problems I was trying to solve were: when I take into consideration annual fees, minimum spends, surcharges, bonus points, spend points and perks, am I actually coming out on top with loyalty points from rewards credit cards? And if so, how can I maximise that benefit? I was also prompted by someone in my 9-5 job saying they didn't trust rewards credit cards and thought it was all a scam, so I was trying to build a proof to show loyalty points and rewards credit cards could provide value. Lastly, I wanted the app to be a good starting point and simple tool for people wanting to get into rewards/loyalty points, by relating everything back to dollars.
I ran beta testing with friends and family, generally the feedback was good from people who already understand how loyalty points work, but people who were wanting to get into points found it confusing. I've launched the app now but am keen to iterate and improve. I want to know if the valuation method survives contact with people who actually know their stuff, whether they get the app, and I guess more broadly whether people think it's even useful to know the cash value of your points. I think it is, because it means when you budget for a holiday you don't need to budget anywhere near as much for flights as if you were paying cash, but keen for other people's opinions.
The point valuation method: instead of quoting one cents-per-point (CPP) number, I sample real award routes and develop a CPP range. Each sample records points required, award taxes, the cash fare for the same flight, and the dates. CPP = (cash fare minus taxes) / points x 100. I've done that across 66 routes for Qantas, 37 for Velocity and 36 for KrisFlyer to get a nice large range. Domestic economy has its own sub-range, international business has its own, gift cards, Points Plus Pay, and so on.
The ranges are wide as the more data points the better. From my sampling so far, 10,000 Qantas points is about $45 if you take a gift card and can be over $400 on the right international economy seat. Bali in economy came out around 1.6c a point. Japan, same cabin, roughly double.
The app has three tools built on this. The 'Value' tool shows what a balance is worth across 17 AU programs split by how you'd redeem. The 'Flight' tool takes a specific flight you're looking at and works out the cpp, then shows where that sits in the benchmark range for that redemption type. And the 'Portfolio' tool is basically an extension of the 'Value' tool, where you can track the value of your points across multiple programs.
Limitations: flights are Qantas, Velocity and KrisFlyer only right now, bank and retail programs are derived from transfer ratios rather than sampled directly, and cash fares move so it's all estimates.
Things I'd like picked apart:
Does a sampled range match how you think about your points, or do you just carry one number in your head? And what would a benchmark need before you'd trust it — more routes, fresher samples, particular route mix? Is the box and whisker chart too complex for the average user to understand? Do you understand the app and how does the UI feel? Also whether splitting Classic and Classic Plus into separate ranges is useful or just noise.
The app is on iOS and Google Play, core tools are free. I don't earn affiliate or referral money from any program or card, and the app doesn't offer financial advice.
Website: https://pointmate.au/ App Store: https://apps.apple.com/app/id6771188233 Google Play: https://play.google.com/store /apps/details?id=au.pointmate.app
